title: Diversifying the Genomic Data Science Research Community
extended_summary:
This perspective paper addresses a structural problem in genomic data science: students and faculty at underserved institutions have historically had limited access to the infrastructure, curricula, mentoring, and funding needed to participate in and contribute to the field. The authors argue that these inequities reduce participation from underrepresented groups and slow the diversification of the genomic data science workforce.

Rather than reporting an empirical intervention study, the paper proposes the Genomic Data Science Community Network (GDSCN) as a coordinated approach to broaden participation. The framework emphasizes several strategies: expanding access to cloud computing and data resources, supporting faculty development, building cross-institution collaborations, recognizing teaching and research contributions, creating student pathways into genomics, developing modular open educational resources, and expanding course-based undergraduate research experiences (CUREs). The paper also highlights pilot efforts such as developing curriculum modules and providing cloud credits through AnVIL.

The context is primarily U.S. higher education, especially community colleges, HBCUs, HSIs, and TCUs, with a focus on faculty, students, and administrators at these institutions as well as R1 collaborators and funders. The main conclusion is that broadening participation in genomic data science requires sustained, multi-level investment in infrastructure, faculty support, student exposure, and funding mechanisms, not isolated one-off programs.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a perspective/position paper on diversifying genomic data science participation and institutional support, not an empirical evaluation of Khanmigo or any K-12 science learning intervention. It contains no study design, no comparison, and no outcome data relevant to direct evidence for K-12 science learning.
impact_tier_rationale: There is no measured impact on learning outcomes or implementation artifacts for Khanmigo or any other educational technology in this paper. The paper is relevant only as background on access and capacity-building in genomics education.
